2016A16.goal: A triangle is reflected in the $x$-axis and then rotated $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin. We need the single transformation that undoes both. Track what happens to a general point $(x,y)$.
2016A16.approach: Compose the two maps on $(x,y)$ to see what the combined transformation is. If it is a reflection, it is its own inverse.

steps.title: Compose
steps.explain: $(x,y)\to(x,-y)\to(-(-y),x)=(y,x)$. So the combined move swaps coordinates: reflection in $y=x$.

steps.title: Undo it
steps.explain: Reflection in $y=x$ undoes itself, so reflecting $\triangle A''B''C''$ in $y=x$ returns $\triangle ABC$.

check.q: What is the inverse of reflection in $y=x$?
check.why: Applying it twice gives the identity.

2016A16.bridge: Compose the two maps on a general point and recognise the result.
solution: The combination is reflection in $y=x$, which is its own inverse.
2016A16.shortcut: Test one vertex: $A(0,2)\to(0,-2)\to(2,0)$; swapping coordinates returns it.
traps: Answering "rotate clockwise $90^\circ$" (that undoes only the rotation).
2016A16.recognize: Compositions of reflections and rotations: compute the effect on $(x,y)$; a reflection followed by a rotation is another reflection.

2016A17.goal: One red ball and $N$ green balls are arranged at random. The red ball's position decides how many greens are on each side. We want the least $N$ (a multiple of $5$) with $P(N)<\tfrac{321}{400}$, where $P$ is the chance that at least $\tfrac35$ of the greens are on one side.

tools.name: Uniform position
tools.fact: \#\text{greens to the left}\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}\text{ each with probability }\tfrac1{N+1}
tools.why: The red ball is equally likely to be in any of the $N+1$ positions.

2016A17.approach: Let $k$ be the number of greens left of red. The condition fails only when $k$ is strictly between $\tfrac{2N}{5}$ and $\tfrac{3N}{5}$. Count those $k$, write $P(N)$, and solve the inequality.

steps.title: Write $P(N)$
steps.explain: With $N=5m$, the condition fails for $k=2m+1,\ldots,3m-1$: $m-1$ values. So $P(N)=1-\tfrac{m-1}{5m+1}$.

2016A17.bridge: Count the failing positions of the red ball and solve for $N$.
solution: With $N=5m$, the condition fails exactly for $2m<k<3m$: $m-1$ of the $5m+1$ equally likely positions.
2016A17.shortcut: Check the given facts: $P(5)=1$ ($m=1$) and $P\to\tfrac45$; this confirms the formula before solving.
traps: Including the endpoints $k=2m$ or $3m$ in the failing set.
Answering $N=480$ instead of its digit sum.
2016A17.recognize: One special object among many: its uniformly random position determines everything.

2016A18.goal: We label a cube's vertices $1$–$8$ so every face has the same sum, counting labellings up to rotation. First the common sum is forced; then the structure is very rigid.

tools.name: Neighbour relation
tools.why: Add the three faces through it and compare with the total $36-L$.

2016A18.approach: Find the face sum. Then show $1$ must be adjacent to $8$ using the neighbour relation. With $8$ and $1$ on an edge, the face equations force the three parallel edges to be $\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}$ with $2,3,5$ on $8$'s side. Count the ways and handle rotations.

steps.title: Face sum and the neighbour relation
steps.explain: $S=\tfrac{3\cdot36}{6}=18$. For a vertex labelled $L$, its three faces give (twice its neighbours) $+$ (its face-diagonal vertices) $=3(18-L)$, while all other vertices total $36-L$. Subtracting: neighbours $-$ opposite $=18-2L$. For $L=8$: neighbours $=$ opposite $+2$.

steps.title: $1$ is next to $8$
steps.explain: If $1$ were opposite $8$, $8$'s neighbours would sum to $3$: impossible. If $1$ were face-diagonal to $8$, combining the relations for $8$ and for $1$ (neighbours $=$ opposite $+16$) forces a label of at least $9$: impossible. So $1$ shares an edge with $8$.

check.q: If $1$ is opposite $8$, what would $8$'s three neighbours sum to?

steps.title: Count
steps.explain: Put $8$ on top and $1$ below it. The two side faces through edge $8$–$1$ force the parallel edges to sum to $9$: pairs $\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}$. The top face needs $8+(\text{three top ends})=18$, so the top ends are $2,3,5$. Assign the three pairs to the three edges: $3!=6$ ways. Placing $8$ and $1$ used up all rotational freedom, so there are $6$ arrangements.

check.q: Which choice of one number from each of $\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}$ sums to $10$?
check.why: $2+3+5=10$; the others are too big or too small.

2016A18.bridge: Get $S=18$, show $1$ is adjacent to $8$, then count assignments of the pairs summing to $9$.
solution: Each vertex is on $3$ faces, so $6S=108$ and $S=18$.
The relation (neighbours) $-$ (opposite) $=18-2L$ rules out $1$ opposite or face-diagonal to $8$, so they share an edge.
The faces through that edge force the three parallel edges to be $\{2,7\},\{3,6\},\{4,5\}$ with $2,3,5$ on $8$'s face.
$3!=6$ assignments, and no rotations remain once $8$ and $1$ are placed.
2016A18.shortcut: Guess the structure "$1$–$8$, $2$–$7$, $3$–$6$, $4$–$5$ on parallel edges" from one example, then count $3!$.
traps: Counting $8!$ labellings divided by $24$ without the face condition.
Forgetting that fixing $8$'s vertex and $1$'s vertex uses all rotations.
2016A18.recognize: Equal-sum labellings of a solid: double count to get the common sum, then derive local relations (neighbours vs opposite) that force the structure.

2016A19.goal: In a $6\times3$ rectangle, $E$ and $F$ trisect $BC$; lines $AE$ and $AF$ cut the diagonal $BD$ at $P$ and $Q$. We want $BP:PQ:QD$. Coordinates make the intersections a matter of solving two linear equations.

tools.name: Parametrise a segment
tools.why: $t$ is the fraction of the way from $B$ to $D$.

2016A19.approach: Parametrise $BD$ by $t$ (fraction from $B$). Find $t$ where it meets $AE$ and $AF$. The ratio $BP:PQ:QD$ is then $t_P:(t_Q-t_P):(1-t_Q)$.
2016A19.bridge: Parametrise $BD$, intersect with $AE$ and $AF$, and read off the ratio.
2016A19.recognize: Ratios along a diagonal cut by lines from a corner: parametrise the diagonal, or use similar triangles with the parallel sides.

2016A20.goal: In the expansion of $(a+b+c+d+1)^N$, we count terms $a^ib^jc^kd^l$ with all exponents positive. Each term is determined by its exponents, with the "$1$" absorbing the remaining degree.

tools.name: Terms of a multinomial
tools.why: Each distinct exponent vector is one term.

tools.name: Stars and bars
tools.why: Subtract $1$ from $i,j,k,l$: $5$ nonnegative variables summing to $N-4$: $\binom{N}{4}$.

2016A20.approach: Count solutions of $i+j+k+l+m=N$ with $i,j,k,l\ge1$, $m\ge0$. Stars and bars gives $\binom N4$. Find $N$ with $\binom N4=1001$.

steps.title: Count the terms
steps.explain: Write $i=i'+1$ etc. Then $i'+j'+k'+l'+m=N-4$ with all $\ge0$: $\binom{(N-4)+4}{4}=\binom N4$.

2016A20.bridge: Count exponent vectors with stars and bars and match $\binom N4=1001$.
solution: Terms with all four variables correspond to $i,j,k,l\ge1$, $m\ge0$ with sum $N$.
2016A20.recognize: "How many terms in the expansion": count exponent vectors with stars and bars.

2016A21.goal: Three circles of radii $1,2,3$ sit on line $l$; the middle one touches both others. We need the area of the triangle of centres. The centres have heights $1,2,3$, so we need their horizontal positions.

tools.name: Horizontal distance between tangent circles on a line
tools.why: Centres differ by $r_1+r_2$ in distance and $|r_1-r_2|$ in height: $d^2=(r_1+r_2)^2-(r_1-r_2)^2=4r_1r_2$.

2016A21.approach: Put $l$ on the $x$-axis and $P$ above the origin. Compute the horizontal gaps $P'Q'$ and $Q'R'$ from the tangency, then use the shoelace formula.

check.q: Circles of radii $1$ and $4$ on a line touch. How far apart are their contact points?

2016A21.bridge: Find the horizontal gaps with $2\sqrt{r_1r_2}$, then use the shoelace formula.
2016A21.shortcut: Memorise $2\sqrt{r_1r_2}$ for circles tangent to each other and to a common line.
2016A21.recognize: Circles resting on a line and touching: horizontal gap $2\sqrt{r_1r_2}$.

2016A22.goal: $110n^3$ has exactly $110$ divisors. We must find the prime factorisation of $n$, then count the divisors of $81n^4$. The divisor-count formula turns this into a factorisation puzzle.
2016A22.approach: Let $n=2^a5^b11^c\cdot(\text{other primes})$. Then $d(110n^3)=(3a+2)(3b+2)(3c+2)\prod(3k+1)=110=2\cdot5\cdot11$. Match factors of the form $3x+2$ to $2,5,11$, and show no other primes fit.

steps.title: Match the factors
steps.explain: $2=3\cdot0+2$, $5=3\cdot1+2$, $11=3\cdot3+2$. So $\{a,b,c\}=\{0,1,3\}$ in some order, and there is no room for other primes (a factor $3k+1\ge4$ would leave too little for three factors $\ge2$).

2016A22.bridge: Write $d(110n^3)$ in terms of $n$'s exponents, match to $2\cdot5\cdot11$, then count for $81n^4$.
solution: So $\{a,b,c\}=\{0,1,3\}$ and $n$ has no other primes.
2016A22.shortcut: The order of $a,b,c$ does not matter for the final count.
2016A22.recognize: Divisor-count equations: express the count via exponents, factor the target, and match forms like $3x+2$.

2016A23.goal: A mystery operation satisfies $a\diamondsuit(b\diamondsuit c)=(a\diamondsuit b)c$ and $a\diamondsuit a=1$. We solve $2016\diamondsuit(6\diamondsuit x)=100$. First find a formula for $a\diamondsuit b$ by plugging in clever values.
2016A23.approach: Use $a\diamondsuit a=1$ to simplify the rule: setting $b=c$ relates $a\diamondsuit b$ to $a\diamondsuit1$, and setting $a=b=c$ gives $a\diamondsuit1=a$. So $a\diamondsuit b=\tfrac ab$.
2016A23.bridge: Plug in equal arguments to find $a\diamondsuit b=\tfrac ab$, then solve.
2016A23.shortcut: Guess $a\diamondsuit b=\tfrac ab$ and verify both rules: $\tfrac{a}{b/c}=\tfrac ab\cdot c$ and $\tfrac aa=1$.
traps: Assuming the operation is subtraction or multiplication.
2016A23.recognize: Functional rules for a strange operation: substitute equal arguments to find a closed form.

2016A24.goal: A cyclic quadrilateral in a circle of radius $200\sqrt2$ has three sides of length $200$. We want the fourth side. Equal chords subtend equal central angles, and the fourth chord's angle is what is left.

tools.name: Chord length
tools.why: Split the isosceles triangle from the centre into two right triangles.

tools.name: Central angles add to $360^circ$
tools.why: The four chords go once around the circle.

2016A24.approach: Find $\sin\tfrac\theta2$ for the side $200$. The fourth chord has central angle $360^\circ-3\theta$, so its length is $2R\sin\tfrac{3\theta}{2}$. Use the triple-angle formula.

check.q: A chord of length $6$ in a circle of radius $5$ has $\sin\tfrac\theta2=$?

steps.title: Fourth chord
steps.explain: Its central angle is $360^\circ-3\theta$, so its length is $2R\sin(180^\circ-\tfrac{3\theta}2)=2R\sin\tfrac{3\theta}2$. With $x=\tfrac\theta2$: $\sin3x=3\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}4-4\cdot\tfrac{2\sqrt2}{64}=\tfrac{3\sqrt2}4-\tfrac{\sqrt2}8=\tfrac{5\sqrt2}8$.

2016A24.bridge: Get $\sin\tfrac\theta2$, use the leftover central angle and the triple-angle formula.
2016A24.shortcut: Ptolemy on a trapezoid also works, but the triple-angle formula is one line.
traps: Assuming the quadrilateral is a square.
2016A24.recognize: Equal chords in a circle: equal central angles; the remaining chord uses the leftover angle.

2016A25.goal: We count positive triples with $\operatorname{lcm}(x,y)=72$, $\operatorname{lcm}(x,z)=600$, $\operatorname{lcm}(y,z)=900$. lcm conditions split prime by prime into conditions on exponents.

tools.name: lcm via exponents
tools.why: The lcm takes the larger power of each prime.

tools.name: Factorisations
tools.why: Read off each prime's required maxima.

2016A25.approach: For each prime $2,3,5$, find the number of exponent triples $(p,q,r)$ for $(x,y,z)$ satisfying the three max conditions. Multiply.

steps.title: Prime 2
steps.explain: $\max(p,q)=3$, $\max(p,r)=3$, $\max(q,r)=2$. So $q,r\le2$, forcing $p=3$, and at least one of $q,r$ is $2$: $9-4=5$ choices.

2016A25.bridge: Handle each prime separately with max conditions on exponents and multiply.
2016A25.shortcut: Whenever one lcm lacks a prime, both of its arguments lack it entirely.
traps: Counting $(q,r)$ pairs with max $\le2$ instead of exactly $2$.
2016A25.recognize: Systems of lcm (or gcd) conditions: go prime by prime with max (or min) conditions on exponents, then multiply.
